URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611204994
SOURCE: Iran International, 20 Nov 2026

Listen to this articleShare An illustration published by the Revolutionary Guards-affiliated Fars News Agency depicts the mythical Persian hero Fereydoun leading a convoy of Iranian oil tankers escorted by warshipsIranian hardliners are calling for a convoy of oil tankers to challenge the US naval blockade, threatening military retaliation against regional energy infrastructure if Washington attempts to stop the vessels.

The proposal, published Thursday by the Revolutionary Guards-affiliated Fars News Agency, calls for tankers to sail to China and threatens strikes on oil facilities in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Qatar if the US intervenes. It emerged shortly after reports that an unsanctioned tanker had been loaded at Iran's Kharg Island oil terminal.

Fars dubbed the plan “Operation Fereydoun,” after a legendary hero in the Persian epic Shahnameh.

No official plans for a convoy have been announced, although Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Iran would break the blockade.

“A blockade is a military action. A military action also has a military response,” political and military analyst Nima Akbarkhani said during a Thursday night discussion on Iranian state television.

Akbarkhani described a previously discussed scenario in which Iranian tankers would sail individually with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals switched on and Iranian flags displayed, while Tehran announced in advance which regional facilities it would target if any vessel were attacked.

During the Be Vaght-e Iran program, host Ruhollah Razavi suggested placing media teams, members of the public and international anti-war activists aboard the tankers to increase the political and media costs of any US intervention.

Akbarkhani endorsed the idea, arguing that unlike vessels sent to Gaza, which Israel prevented from reaching their destination despite extensive media coverage, Iran could deter attacks on blockade-breaking tankers by threatening military retaliation.

Support for confrontation grows

Political analyst Mostafa Najafi, recently described in Iranian media as an adviser to Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, wrote on X that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had ordered an end to the “neither war nor peace” situation some time ago.

Najafi suggested that the effort extended beyond diplomacy, with military options also under consideration.

“Apparently, Tehran no longer wants to sit back and watch the blockade and threats,” he wrote.

Majid-Reza Hariri, president of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce, called on Iranians across the political spectrum to support efforts to break the blockade.

“After months of pursuing negotiations in various ways, every Iranian patriot, regardless of political outlook, should support the government in breaking the naval blockade imposed by the aggressive United States by any means possible,” he wrote Friday.

Media analyst Alireza Shiva argued that Iran was signaling that energy security in the Persian Gulf could not be defined unilaterally.

“You cannot target Iran's oil exports while expecting the energy exports of others to continue in complete security,” he wrote on X.

Hardline journalist Parisa Nasr argued that Iran had made a strategic mistake by treating the blockade as a negotiating issue rather than a wartime measure intended to weaken the country and force its surrender.

She advocated a strategy of “bringing the crisis to the brink” to pressure Washington into easing the blockade while strengthening Iran's deterrence against attacks on its tankers.

Energy analyst Abdullah Babakhani offered a more cautious assessment, suggesting that US forces might initially allow some Iranian tankers through before pursuing and potentially seizing them in international waters.

He compared the scenario to operations involving the pursuit and seizure of tankers linked to Venezuela last year, saying Iran's response to such an eventuality remained unpredictable.

China, Iran's largest oil buyer before the blockade, has been identified as the intended destination for the proposed convoy. Whether Beijing would accept the shipments remains unclear.

The proposal therefore presents Tehran with a potentially consequential choice: continue seeking a negotiated end to the blockade or test Washington's willingness to enforce it at the risk of a wider military confrontation.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesWho is Mohammad Javad Bavand, the ex-IRGC official sanctioned by US?Nov 21, 2026, 00:10 GMT+0Listen to this article100%Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence official sanctioned by the United States on Friday, has played a key role in Iran's sanctioned oil trade, working through a network of intermediaries to sell crude and recover revenues held abroad.

The US Treasury sanctioned Bavand alongside three other Iranians — Majid Taj, Mojtaba Arabnejad and Mohammadhossein Servati — over their roles in networks supporting Iran's oil trade and sanctions evasion.

The Treasury said Bavand worked with intermediaries, including Taj, the brother of Iranian Football Federation president Mehdi Taj, to recover proceeds from Iranian oil sales held abroad, despite members of the network owing billions of dollars from previous transactions.

Iran International investigations have documented Bavand's rise from the Revolutionary Guards Intelligence Organization to senior positions overseeing oil sales, including the allocation of millions of barrels of crude to intermediaries with billions of dollars in outstanding debts.

From intelligence officer to oil trader

Bavand previously served as deputy head of the economic directorate of the Revolutionary Guards Intelligence Organization under Mostafa Ahadi.

Following the US withdrawal from the nuclear agreement in 2018, he represented Guards intelligence on a Supreme National Security Council committee responsible for overseeing sanctioned oil sales.

He later became a special assistant to the oil minister under former President Ebrahim Raisi. After leaving the position under President Masoud Pezeshkian, Bavand returned to the Oil Ministry in June 2026 to oversee oil trading.

Millions of barrels entrusted to indebted traders

In September, Iran International published confidential documents raising questions about the allocation of sanctioned crude to four intermediaries who had failed to return billions of dollars from earlier sales.

The documents showed that the traders were offered unusually steep discounts despite their outstanding debts.

A subsequent investigation found that Bavand and oil-trading official Ali Akbar Pour-Ebrahim had assigned 86 million barrels of Iranian crude to four intermediaries, including Hossein Shamkhani and Mohammad Hadi Momenin.

The findings formed part of Iran International's reporting on a struggle between networks linked to the Revolutionary Guards Intelligence Organization and the Intelligence Ministry for control of Iran's sanctioned oil trade.

A November 9 investigation revealed further details of Iran's efforts to use oil terminals and storage facilities in China to circumvent US sanctions.

It cited an earlier document showing that Bavand had instructed Momenin, an oil intermediary who owed $2 billion in outstanding proceeds, to use a vessel linked to Hossein Shamkhani to deliver oil for storage at a Chinese port.

Treasury names Bavand's associates

The Treasury said Bavand had worked with the Revolutionary Guards and Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars, a previously sanctioned company tasked with selling oil for Iran's Armed Forces General Staff.

Its designation of Majid Taj also brought renewed attention to a relationship documented in Iran International's earlier investigations into the oil-trading network.

Bavand and Taj were sanctioned under Executive Order 13902, which targets designated sectors of Iran's economy. Arabnejad, who was linked to Mahan Air, and Servati, who was linked to Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars, were sanctioned under counterterrorism-related authorities.

The measures block any assets the four hold under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit Americans from conducting transactions with them.

Listen to this article100%Traffic moves along a smog-covered highway near Tehran's Azadi Tower, as air pollution blankets the Iranian capital, November 18, 2026Iran faces a worsening winter energy crisis after wartime damage to its gas infrastructure cut production capacity, with officials warning of shortages in 11 provinces and limited options to make up the shortfall.

The country's daily gas deficit, estimated at around 300 million cubic metres last winter, is expected to reach 430 million cubic metres this winter.

Mohammad Sadegh Azimifar, head of the National Iranian Oil Products Distribution Company (NIOPDC), has announced that 60 million litres of kerosene have been stockpiled in some provinces facing severe gas shortages.
